chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Sa'd ibn Abi Khalaf, who said:

I asked Abu Al-Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) about something from the divorce. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'When a man divorces his wife with a divorce in which he has no control regarding the reversion, so she is irrevocably divorced from him the moment he divorces her, and she is in control of herself, and there is no way for him upon her, and she waits wherever she desires, and there is no expenses for her.'
I said: 'Is not Allah, Mighty and Majestic, Saying: Do not drive them out of their houses, nor should they themselves go forth?'

So he (peace be upon him) said: 'But rather it Means by that who is divorced with a divorce after a divorce, so she is the one who should not be driven out nor go out until she is divorced by the third divorce. So when she is divorced with the third, so she is irrevocably divorced from him, and there is no expenses for her.'

And the woman whom the man divorces with a divorce, then leaves her until her term is free, so this one as well should sit in the house of her husband, and for her is the expenses, and the dwelling until she fulfills her waiting period.'
ai.seo_question: Where does a divorced woman wait during her iddah and is she entitled to maintenance?
ai.summary: Imam Musa al-Kadhim (AS) clarifies that the Quranic command 'do not drive them out' specifically applies to revocable divorces (talaq raj'i) where the husband retains the right of reversion, ensuring the wife's right to housing and maintenance. In contrast, for irrevocable divorces (talaq ba'in) or khula', the wife is considered fully separated and may reside wherever she chooses without financial support from the husband. This distinction highlights the Shia jurisprudential nuance that the verse's protection is conditional upon the potential for reconciliation.
